verdict: Retested desolvation the RIGHT way — real Shrake-Rupley SASA (bound vs unbound) for the burial, plus the SATISFACTION correction the proposal describes: a buried polar/charged atom is only taxed when it has NO H-bond/salt partner across the interface. This directly fixes what my earlier CRUDE occlusion desolvation missed (that one applied a blanket polar penalty and HURT the model, 0.528->0.515). Measured on the complex-held-out alanine task (n=1156): the individual components behave as the physics predicts — hydrophobic-buried area tracks ΔΔG at r +0.38 (burying oily surface contributes binding), and critically the UNSATISFIED-polar-buried area carries its own signal (r -0.05), distinct from satisfied-polar burial (r +0.25) — the illusion correction separates the two, which the crude term could not. On the held-out predictor: baseline 0.522; + crude occlusion desolv 0.532 (+0.010); + EEF1 SASA-with-satisfaction 0.522 (+0.000). HONEST OUTCOME: even done properly, on THIS alanine-heavy held-out validation the EEF1-with-satisfaction term does not materially beat the baseline (+0.000) — its burial signal is still largely already captured by the vdW + buried-contact features, and the alanine scan (which removes a sidechain entirely) is a weak place for a desolvation term to add orthogonal value. It is a better, more physical term than the crude one (and no longer HURTS), but it is not a headline accuracy win here. Reported, not dressed up. Compute cost: real SASA adds ~0.5-1s per complex (Shrake-Rupley), cached per complex.
